newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia economy seen little affected by election.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia economy seen little affected by election.

text.p: The Indonesian general election campaign that opened on Sunday is expected to have little affect on the nation's economy, but short-term nervousness in financial markets over possible unrest will continue, economists said.

Despite unfavourable publicity over the Busang gold property and recent reports that it is one of the most corrupt countries in the world, economists said Indonesia was the investment destination of choice in fast-growing Southeast Asia.
They told Reuters that despite simmering political tensions in Indonesia, the election process would not sully that image.

"Economic growth is going to remain strong over the coming years," said Desmond Supple, an economist at BZW Barclays in Singapore. "Inflation is likely to pick up later this year, but nothing too dramatic by historic standards. We are seeing a stronger economy.

"Economic policy will not be altered by the election," Supple said. But, "when you talk about international investor confidence in Indonesia, it is always a political situation. That's always the albatross around the neck."
"Political concerns are always a perennial bugbear for the Indonesian rupiah. They remain in place at the moment over the election period," he said.

The rupiah plunged on Thursday and Friday, dropping some 20 points to 2,440.50 against the dollar, as nervous investors fearing violence during the campaign sold off the currency. It later recovered to 2,435.00/37.00 by Saturday.

The stock market has been little affected, but brokers said there was some profit-taking on Friday that could be attributed to pre-election nervousness. The composite index closed down 0.08 percent at 652.48 points.
The government has predicted economic growth of 7.5 to 7.8 percent in 1997 against 7.82 percent in 1996. Inflation is pegged at between 5-6 percent against 6.47 percent in 1996.
Economists said those numbers were good and spoke of an underlying strength in the economy, which was not easily susceptible to pressure.

"Fluctuations in currency, such as those this last week, are not an economic indicator," said J.W. Taco Bottema, an economist of the Economic and Social Commission for Asia and the Pacific. "Day-to-day ripples are rarely a sign of any structural changes."

Other analysts said the results of the May 29 election were a foregone conclusion -- the ruling Golkar party is expected to coast to victory -- and that any sporadic violence during the campaign would have only a temporary effect.

"Economic policy will not be altered by the election results," said Supple, adding that the one drawback he saw in the economy -- a fall in labour productivity -- was being addressed by the government.
"There is a reliance on light manufacturing and labour-intensive industries," he said.

"Indonesia is not internationally competitive in those sectors any more. There is a need to upgrade the export sector into more value-added areas. The government is addressing that issue and is encouraging investment into those sectors. So the overall trend is very encouraging."

Economists said the Busang gold property controversy, in which the owners Bre-X Minerals Ltd were advised by the government to sell a 55 percent stake to Indonesian interests and Freeport McMoRan Cooper and Gold Inc, would have little overall effect on investor confidence.
The project has now sunk deeper into controversy with doubts raised over the veracity of Bre-X's earlier estimates that it was the biggest gold find this century.
The economists said a report by the Hong Kong-based Political and Economic Risk Consultancy that Indonesia was the most corrupt country in Asia was also largely discounted.

"Busang may or may not be a lump of gold out there somewhere," said one diplomat. "What investors are looking at is that this is a country of 200 million people with a per capita income of over $1,000. That's the bottom line."
